title: Adapter: integrate a third-party payment gateway with your system's interface.
keyPoints: The Adapter pattern translates a foreign interface into the one your code expects, so incompatible classes collaborate without coupling.
The client depends on its own clean target interface; the adapter implements it and delegates to the third-party class.
Swapping one payment provider for another means writing a new adapter, not editing business logic.
The adapter is the right place to normalise error codes, currency units, idempotency keys, and retry semantics.
Dependency Inversion is satisfied because the client depends on its own abstraction, not on the vendor.
Open/Closed is satisfied because a new provider is a new adapter with zero changes to existing callers.

s1_definition.oneliner: The Adapter pattern translates a foreign interface into the one your code expects, so incompatible classes collaborate without coupling.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Adapter** – converts the interface of a class into another interface the client expects, allowing incompatible classes to work together.
- **Target interface** – the clean interface defined by the client system, for example `PaymentProcessor`.
- **Adaptee** – the third-party or legacy class with an incompatible API, for example `RazorpayGateway`.
- **Adapter class** – implements the target interface and holds an instance of the adaptee, translating every call.
- **Isolation** – the client never references the vendor directly, so swapping providers means writing a new adapter.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the Adapter as a plug converter at National Bank of India when integrating an outside payment gateway. The bank's code speaks one standard "pay" language, but the Razorpay gateway speaks its own. The adapter is the travel plug that sits between them, so when Rajesh pays, the bank calls its own standard method and the adapter quietly translates it into whatever Razorpay actually expects.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Business Code (depends on PaymentProcessor)
       │
       │  processor.pay(accountId, amount)
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │       RazorpayAdapter            │
  │  implements PaymentProcessor     │
  │                                  │
  │  Converts: rupees → paise        │
  │  Maps: accountId → merchantRef   │
  │  Adapts: RazorpayResponse →      │
  │          PaymentResult           │
  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │       RazorpayGateway            │
  │  (third-party, incompatible)     │
  │  charge(RazorpayRequest)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

```text
  Swapping providers:

  Before: PaymentProcessor → RazorpayAdapter → RazorpayGateway
  After:  PaymentProcessor → StripeAdapter   → StripeGateway

  Business code is IDENTICAL in both cases
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Adapter pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface the client expects, so two otherwise incompatible pieces can work together. Rajesh uses it constantly when integrating third-party or legacy systems, because the bank's own code should speak one clean, stable language and never be shaped by a vendor's API.

The structure is a target interface that the system defines, for example a `PaymentProcessor` with a simple `pay` method, and an adapter that implements that target while holding an instance of the foreign class. The adapter translates each call: it maps the arguments, converts data formats like rupees to paise, and normalises the response, so the business code calls its own method and the adapter quietly does whatever the vendor requires underneath.

The decisive benefit is isolation. Because the bank's code depends only on its own `PaymentProcessor` interface and never references the vendor directly, switching from Razorpay to Stripe means writing a new adapter rather than editing business logic. This satisfies both Dependency Inversion and Open/Closed. The provider change does not ripple through the codebase.

The senior insight is that the adapter is the perfect place to tame the messy realities of external APIs: different error codes, currency units, idempotency keys, and retry semantics. Everything behind the adapter sees one consistent, well-behaved interface. At National Bank of India, wrapping a payment gateway behind an adapter is what lets the team onboard or swap a provider by writing one class, while the payment flow that has already been tested and audited stays completely untouched.

Remember one sentence: the Adapter translates a foreign interface into your own, isolating vendor quirks so business code never knows which provider is behind it.
